title: Biological valorization of methane and nitrogen gas-derived ammonia via methanotrophic bacteria for gut-beneficial nutrients

paper_content.abstract:
The in-situ upcycling of decentralized methane and nitrogen gas (N )-derived ammonia via
2
methanotrophic bacteria is highly attractive. However, the toxic intermediate generated from
ammonia oxidation significantly inhibits cell growth, thereby hindering efficient bioproduction.
Herein, by integrating transcriptomic analysis, we develop rational metabolic engineering
strategies and an optimized fed-batch fermentation to enhance ammonia utilization in a
methanotrophic bacterium of Methylotuvimicrobium sanxanigenens. The modified M.
sanxanigenens overexpressing hydroxylamine reductase efficienStly co-assimilates methane and
ammonia for cell protein synthesis, with an 18-fold increase in productivity. The resulting
methanotrophic cell protein (MCP) not only exhibits an Rideal essential amino acid profile but also
contains bioactive nutrients, including polysaccharides and peptides. Oral administration of this
nutritional MCP significantly ameliorates colitis symptoms in male mice by attenuating
inflammatory progression and restoring the intestinal barrier. Moreover, MCP treatment maintains
gut microbiota homeostasis and promotes the excretion of beneficial metabolites, thereby
protecting the intestinal microeInvironment. Hence, this study provides a promising biological
approach for the local bioR-valorization of decentralized CH
4
and air into functional feed additives.
This biotechnology not only facilitates advancements in developing carbon-negative gas-to-value
pathways but also drives green transformations in animal husbandry by reducing the use of
antibiotics and vaccines.
paper_content.introduction:
China has abundant decentralized methane (CH ) derived from fossil fuel extraction and organic
4
waste treatment processes.1,2 However, it is difficult and costly to collect these CH resources via
4
pipelines and upgrade them for natural gas production. Thus, decentralized CH is often combusted
4
for low-value heat and power to meet the energy demands of surrounding factories, ultimately
resulting in the complete waste of carbon resources. Aerobic methanotrophic bacteria, however,
can utilize CH to synthesize single cell protein as an alternative feed additive.3 This approach may
4
not only valorize decentralized CH but also alleviate protein shorStages—a critical issue given that
4
S
more than 80% of China’s soybean and fishmeal supplies rely on imports, totaling over 100 million
E
tons annually.4 This context underscores the urgent need Rto develop efficient biological approaches
P
for valorizing decentralized CH₄ into protein feed, thus addressing both carbon resource waste and
N
protein supply challenges.
I
E
L
This biological upcycling of decentralized CH is technically feasible, as mature technologies exist
4
C
for supplying key nutrients. As oIne of the most widely used nitrogen sources in biomanufacturing,
T
ammonia can be produceRd from nitrogen gas (N
2
) via an efficient and environmentally friendly
A
photo-electrocatalytic (PEC) process.5 Cryogenic distillation, a well-established technology in the
chemical industry, separates high-purity N from air. Under the assumed conditions
2
(Supplementary Note 1), this process also co-produces high-purity oxygen gas (O ).6 Therefore,
2
simultaneous utilization of O generated from both air separation unit (ASU) operations and the
2
PEC process enables maximal O utilization, as O serves as a crucial substrate for methanotrophic
2 2
bacteria.3 Detailed balanced reactions and corresponding calculations are provided in
Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Note 3. Moreover, the single cell protein produced can
be processed into microbial nutrients and formulated into animal feed, directly supporting nearby
livestock farms. This integrated supply chain—where air-derived O₂ and green ammonia support
CH₄-based microbial protein synthesis—lays a solid technical foundation for the sustainable, local
upcycling of decentralized CH₄.

However, several vital issues must be addressed to fully realize this prospect. First, methanotrophic
bacteria are not natural consumers of ammonia. Notably, it is widely reported that ammonia is
partially oxidized by methane monooxygenase (MMO) to form a highly toxic intermediate,
hydroxylamine—a compound that significantly impairs the growth of aerobic methanotrophic
bacteria.7 Given the difficulty in modifying MMO’s selectivity toward ammonia without
compromising its methane oxidation activity, there is an urgent need to investigate the mechanisms
underlying deficient ammonia utilization by integrating omics analysis. This serves as a
S
prerequisite for designing rational strategies to overcome metaSbolic bottlenecks in hydroxylamine
E
detoxification. Furthermore, although several studies have shown that methanotrophic bacterium-
R
derived cell protein promotes intestinal health iPn fish,8,9 its biofunctions and associated
mechanisms remain underexplored in standarNdized animal models. This currently restricts its
I
application as a bulk protein substitute—im peding its ability to compete with traditional feeds and
E
gain acceptance from markets and coLnsumers.10 These challenges greatly hamper endeavors to
C
establish proof of concept for the in-situ valorization of decentralized CH₄.
I
T
R
In this study, we seleAct Methylotuvimicrobium sanxanigenens NG09 (CGMCC No. 30951)—a
methanotrophic bacterium isolated from rice paddies with a high growth rate—as a CH -utilizing
4
cell factory.11 To clarify the mechanism of its growth inhibition by ammonia, we perform a
transcriptomic analysis to identify key enzymes involved in hydroxylamine detoxification. Based
on these findings, we rationally construct the engineered strain SO01 overexpressing
hydroxylamine reductase to enhance its growth with ammonia as the sole nitrogen source (Figure
1). We further develop a fed-batch fermentation strategy to match the ammonia production
capacity of upstream N fixation with the downstream growth demands of strain SO01. To expand
2
the applications beyond a mere protein substitute, we investigate the effects of the produced
microbial nutrients on attenuating dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis in mice.
We observe that these microbial nutrients also protect the intestinal microenvironment in mice, as
evidenced by the recovery of gut microbiota diversity and the promotion of prebiotic excretion.
Our work thus highlights the prospect of biovalorizing decentralized CH and air into value-added
4
functional animal nutrients.

methanotrophic chassis
Methanotrophic cultivation typically relies on nitrate as nitrogen Ssource,12,13 primarily due to the
S
severe growth inhibition associated with ammonia utilization. Given that the cost of nitrate salts is
E
approximately twice that of ammonia,14 it is thus crucial Rto endow methanotrophic bacterial chassis
P
with enhanced ammonia utilization capacity. Although ammonia is the preferred nitrogen source
N
for protein biosynthesis in most microorganisms, it is partially oxidized by MMO to form toxic
I
hydroxylamine, which significantly hampers cell growth. We firstly tested the growth ability of M.
E
sanxanigenens NG09 with ammonia (for the remainder of this manuscript, molecular ammonia
L
(NH ) and ionic ammonium (NHI+) salt are collectively referred to as “ammonia” for consistency).
3 4
C
Similar to other methanRotrophic species,15 M. sanxanigenens NG09 cultured with ammonia
T
exhibited a 12-h longer lag phase than when grown with nitrate (Figure 2a)—a nitrogen source
A
widely used in methanotrophic bacteria cultures. This indicated that the cells may experience an
adaption period for utilizing ammonia. Additionally, M. sanxanigenens NG09 firstly utilized
ammonia when both two nitrogen sources existed, and nitrate uptake was observed only after
ammonia depletion (Supplementary Figure 1 and Supplementary Note 4).

To clarify the underlying mechanisms of ammonia preference and related growth retardation, we
sought to find evidence from whole-genome transcriptional responses of M. sanxanigenens NG09
grown in the exponential phase. This approach enables the identification of key detoxification-
related enzymes, which in turn facilitates the development of a rational genetic modification
strategy to enhance cellular ammonia utilization. In the PCA analysis, the principal component 1
explained 95% of the variation (Figure 2b). High correlations among samples within groups,
together with weak correlations among different groups (Supplementary Figure 2a–b), indicated
that the type of nitrogen source was the prominent cause of changes in gene transcription.
Compared with growth with nitrate, 121 and 150 genes were significantly up- and down-regulated
in the ammonia culture (Supplementary Figure 2c–d), respectively.

As ammonia toxicity is proposed to be highly relevant to the formation of hydroxylamine, we then
focused on the 45 differentially expressed genes involved in the nitrogen metabolism. The genes
encoding nitrate reductase (nar), nitrate transport proteins (nrtASBC), and nitrite reductases (nirBD
and nir) were all repressed in cultures with ammonia (Figure 2c). This explained the phenomenon
of
blocked nitrate uptake when ammonia existed. APdditionally, N fixation, urea and cyanate
2
assimilation pathways were all inactivated (SuppNlementary Data 1). These changes were consistent
I
with the fact that ammonia is the preferred nitrogen source with the lowest energy and reducing
E
power demand.16 However, when M. sLanxanigenens NG09 was cultured with ammonia, the genes
C
encoding hydroxylamine reductase (har) and dehydrogenase subunits (haoAB) were significantly
I
T
up-regulated by 3.9-, 3.8- and 3.3-fold, respectively. This transcriptional response indicates that
R
the strain was subjecteAd to hydroxylamine-induced toxicity, a conclusion further supported by the
detection of 70.5 μM hydroxylamine per unit cell density (OD ) in the ammonia-fed culture
600
(Supplementary Figure 3). By contrast, no hydroxylamine was detected in the nitrate cultures,
which can be attributed to the absence of hydroxylamine-generating steps in the nitrate
assimilation pathway.17,18 Correspondingly, M. sanxanigenens NG09 accumulates 3.34 mg of
NO −-N L−1 in the ammonia-based cultures, an approximately 10-fold higher than that measured
2
in the nitrate-grown cultures (0.33 mg NO −-N L−1, Supplementary Figure 4). Together, the
2

of M. sanxanigenens NG09 when the nitrogen source was switched to ammonia.

We further designed metabolic engineering strategies to redirect hydroxylamine flux. The haoAB-
deficient strain showed severely impaired growth with ammonia (Supplementary Figure 5 and
Supplementary Note 5), indicating that hydroxylamine dehydrogenase is important for
detoxification. Additionally, as nitrite reductases were all repressed under ammonia culture, nitrite
accumulated due to enhanced hydroxylamine oxidation, thus hampering cellular metabolic
activities. However, negligible improvement of cell growth was observed by overexpressing
hydroxylamine dehydrogenase or two nitrite reductases (Supplementary Figure 6 and
Supplementary Note 6). Moreover, in order to alleviate the growth retardation, we also attempted
to regulate intracellular ammonia availability by eliminating the transporters. Nonetheless,
knockout of amtA and/or amtB did not notably affect the Slag phase and growth rate of the
engineered strains grown with ammonia. The NH +-N level exhibits no significant differences (p >

sanxanigenens NG09 is not limited by amNmonia transport (Supplementary Figure 7 and

Another strategy is toA upregulate the transcriptional level of hydroxylamine reductase, which
catalyzes the direct hydroxylamine reduction to ammonia. On the basis of per mole hydroxylamine

The inducer arabinose exerts no significant impact on growth at concentrations below 0.5 g L−1
and is not assimilated by methanotrophic bacteria.19 Given its superior growth performance with
ammonia (Figure 2d−e), M. sanxanigenens SO01 was selected for subsequent cultivations, with
arabinose added at 0.1 g L−1 to induce har expression. When M. sanxanigenens SO01 was cultured
with ammonia and supplemented with 0.1 g L−1 arabinose to induce har expression, the

In contrast, arabinose concentrations of 0.25 and 0.4 g L−1 impose an enhanced metabolic burden,
leading to cellular resource reallocation and slowed cell growth as a compensatory adaptation
(Figure 2d).20 Consequently, these higher concentrations fail to yield significant improvements in
har expression and even impair the growth of M. sanxanigenens SO01. In summary, the ammonia-
based growth capacity of M. sanxanigenens is enhanced by reinforcing direct hydroxylamine
reduction.

Pronounced growth inhibition of the hLar-overexpressing M. sanxanigenens SO01 occurred when

Note 8). However, more ammonia is required to achieve substantial cell protein production without
impairing growth. SuAbsequently, a fed-batch strategy was established, and the cell density
increased by nearly 70% when ammonia concentration did not exceed 10 mM (Supplementary
Figure 10), consistent with the results of ammonia tolerance test. In contrast, a rapid growth decline
occurred at 36 h in the high-dose cultivation. Therefore, further fed-batch cultivation was
conducted to control the ammonia concentration below 10 mM.

(CUR), and highest DCW were 17.68, 33.60 mmol L−1 h−1, and 5.30 g L−1 (Figure 3c−d and

g DCW g−1 N, respectively (Supplementary Tables 3−4, equation 1−2). On the other hand, the

(Supplementary Figure 14f). The corresponding metPhane- and nitrogen-based yields were 0.94 g

4

We further characterized the cell protLein of the engineered M. sanxanigenens strain. The protein
and polysaccharide contents reached 347 and 429 mg g−1 DCW, respectively, collectively
accounting for approximately 70%–80% of the DCW (Figure 3d). The isoleucine and leucine
contents of the methanotrophic cell protein (MCP) were 94.7% and 93.4% of those in whole egg,
while the valine content was comparable to that in whole egg and cow milk (Figure 3e and
Supplementary Figure 15).22 The branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) content of MCP was 10.9%
higher than that in fishmeal and closely matched that of whole egg (Figure 3f).23 Additionally, the
essential amino acid (EAA) content of MCP reached 107.1% of that in fishmeal. These results
indicate that the nutritional value of MCP is comparable to that of fishmeal, whole egg, and cow
milk. A minor yet significant intracellular peptide mixture was also identified (inset of Figure 3f),
which was reported to exhibit anti-inflammation effects and protect animal intestinal microbiota.24
Furthermore, the safety of this nutritional cell protein was verified, with an endotoxin level below
0.02 EU mL−1. Thus, our methanotrophic cell protein contains diverse nutrients and bioactive
peptides, highlighting its potential application as a functional feed additive.

Probiotic effects of nutritional cell protein on gut health
Recent studies have emphasized the promising benefits of MCP in promoting fish gut health. Here,
we employed a dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis mouse model, which adequately
simulated key pathological features of intestinal inflammation (relevant to human intestinal
disorders), including intestinal barrier disruption, inflammatory response, and gut microbiota
dysbiosis. The MCP was orally administered to evaluate its efficacy in ameliorating DSS-induced
colitis (Supplementary Figure 16 and Supplementary Figure 17a). Compared to the model group
(“+DSS” group), colitis mice treated with MCP (“+DSS,MCSP” group) exhibited significantly
reduced body weight loss (Figure 4a), lower disease activity index (DAI) score (Figure 4b and
Supplementary Table 5), and less colon shortening P(Figure 4c and Supplementary Figure 17c),
thereby contributing to a higher survival rate (SNupplementary Figure 17b).

The maintenance of the intestinal baLrrier integrity is critical for gut health.25 MCP treatment
mitigated DSS-induced structural integrity disruption of colonic tissue, as evidenced by reducing
mucosal ulceration, crypt damage, and inflammatory cell infiltration (Figure 4d, Supplementary
Table 6 and SupplemenAtary Data 2). Notably, the tight junction protein Occludin, which is essential
for maintaining the intestinal epithelial barrier, was markedly restored upon treatment with the
MCP (Figure 4e and Supplementary Figure 17d). Furthermore, the MCP demonstrated a
significant inhibitory effect on the protein expression of pro-inflammatory interleukin-6 (IL-6) and
tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) (Figure 4f and Supplementary Figure 18a–c), and restored the
expression of anti-inflammatory interleukin-10 (IL-10) compared to mice with colitis (Figure 4g
and Supplementary Figure 18d). These findings indicated that administration of MCP helped to
alleviate colitis by restoring intestinal barrier and attenuating inflammations in mice.

Nutritional cell protein protects intestinal health by modulating microenvironment
As MCP produced from CH and N -derived ammonia effectively ameliorated the inflammatory
4 2
bowel disease symptoms in mice, 16s rRNA gene sequencing was conducted to assess the effect
of MCP on intestinal microbiota (Supplementary Figure 19a). Administration of MCP significantly
increased the gut microbiota diversity in mice with colitis (Figure 5a–b and Supplementary Figure
19b–c). Additionally, the microbiota of mice treated with the MCP closely resembled that of the
healthy control group (Supplementary Figure 19d and Supplementary Note 10).

DSS treatment led to severe dysbiosis of the mice gut microbiota, which was effectively reversed
by MCP administration (Supplementary Figure 20 and Supplementary Note 11). MCP gavage
remarkably reduced the abundance of Campylobacterota, a phSylum associated with inflammation
(Figure 5c and Supplementary Figure 20b). Pathogenic genera, including Klebsiella, Enterocloster,
Muribaculum, and Helicobacter, proliferated in micPe with DSS-induced colitis, whereas MCP
treatment inhibited these pathogens and incrNeased the abundance of short-chain fatty acid-
producing probiotics, such as Alloprevote lla and Kineothrix (Supplementary Figure 20d and
Supplementary Figure 21a). At the sLpecies level, we observed a proportional rise in the anti-
inflammatory bacteria Faecalibaculum rodentium and Odoribacter laneu, while the disease-
related Helicobacter ganmani was suppressed following MCP intake (Supplementary Figure 21b
and Supplementary NoAte 12).

The recovery of the microbiota diversity may improve the distribution of metabolites and thus
contribute to the maintenance of the intestinal homeostasis. We conducted further investigations
on fecal metabolites in mice (Supplementary Figure 22–23 and Supplementary Note 13–14).
Treatment with the MCP resulted in a notable increase in prebiotic excretion including
taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA) and suberic acid, compared to the model group (Figure 5d).
TCDCA, previously reported to alleviate intestinal inflammation,26 exhibited the highest area
under the curve in a receiver operating characteristic analysis (Supplementary Figure 24 and
Supplementary Note 15). Additionally, suberic acid level significantly decreased in mice with
colitis, and was markedly elevated after MCP administration (Supplementary Table 7 and
Supplementary Data 3). This compound is highly correlated with enrichments of gut beneficial
bacteria.27 Therefore, these two metabolites were speculated as the biomarkers for attenuation of
mouse colitis through MCP treatment. To sum up, these results highlight that oral administration
of MCP assisted in mitigating mouse colitis progression by positively modulating intestinal
microbiota and enhancing prebiotics excretion.

Additionally, it is noteworthy that MCP treatment also benefits healthy mice by protecting the gut
microenvironment. This was evidenced by a boosted expression of Occludin with MCP
administration (Figure 4e, “−DSS,MCP” group versus “S−DSS” group). Furthermore, the
abundance of 11 bacterial taxa significantly increased among mice treated with MCP, including
the probiotic Lactobacillaceae, Lacticaseibacillus, anPd Prevotellaceae (Figure 5e). The MCP also
dramatically enhanced the excretion of beneficiaNl metabolites, including isovaleric acid, L-alanine,
lithocholic acid acetate, and myristic acid, in comparison to the normal mice (“−DSS” group)
(Figure 5f). Overall, our results suggesLt the potential use of MCP as a nutritional additive to prevent
inflammatory bowel disease in healthy animals.

Strain and culture conditions

LC-MS analysis of 15N labeled amino acids
Protein samples (two bAiologically independent replicates) were subjected to acid hydrolysis (6 N
HCl, 110 ℃,24 h) to liberate free amino acids. The hydrolysate supernatants (1 mL) were dried

Metabolic flux analysis was performed using a Thermo ScientificQ Exactive HF-X hybrid
quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometer coupled to a UHPLC system. Chromatographic separation
was achieved on an ACQUITY UPLC BEH Amide column (2.1 mm x 100 mm, 1.7 m; Waters)
maintained at 30℃. The mobile phase consisted of ammonium acetate buffer (solvent A) and
acetonitrile (solvent B). The gradient elution was performed at a flow rate of 0.4 mL mL–1 as
follows: 0–0.5 min, 95% B; 0.5–7 min, 95% to 65% B; 7-8 min, 65% to 50% B; 8–9 min, 50% B;
9–9.1 min 50% to 95% B; and 9.1–12 min, 95% B.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
General Comments:
In this study the authors present a sequence of approaches. They begin by introducing the use of air-derived ammonia for
methanotrophic growth, but this part relies on a previously published technology from another group rather than a new
experimental demonstration. They then perform transcriptomic analysis to show that ammonia is toxic, and attempt to
address this by overexpressing hao under arabinose induction. Although this led to higher biomass, toxicity still persisted
above 10 mM ammonia. Next, they conduct a fed-batch fermentation strategy in which ammonia was maintained below 10
mM, allowing significant biomass production. The resulting biomass was characterized in terms of amino acid composition
and tested in a DSS-induced colitis mouse model, where it showed improvement in gut microbiota.
The following comments need to be address for this manuscript.
Specific comments:
1. Line 103: The stated PEC stoichiometry (2 NH3 : 1.5 O2) equals 0.75 mol O2 per mol NH3, not 0.9. Please correct this
and use consistent units. If 0.9 derives from another PEC route, provide the balanced reaction and calculation.
2. Line 105: 1:1 nitrogen source/O2 uptake” is ambiguous. Please specify the basis and units (e.g., mol N fed vs mol O2
consumed, per time or per biomass), and provide a numerical example. Also note that in the cited paper by Fei et. al
continuous cultures are nitrate-fed, not ammonia-fed, please state this explicitly.
3. Line 107–112: Author’s conclude PEC + air separation can supply O2 and NH3, but no calculation is shown. Please
include a short example using your 3-L run data to estimate O2 uptake and N demand.
4. Line 100: “1 mol N2 with 0.3 mol O2” is not fixed. ASUs deliver independent streams. Please clarify the technology and
recovery assumptions.
5. Section “Assessing production of cell mass from CH4 and N2-derived ammonia” reads more like methods/assumptions
than results and cannot stand alone as a results subsection. Also, since actual runs used external aeration and NH4Cl feed,
please add a clarifying sentence to avoid reader confusion.
6. Line 107: Replace balance with adequate.
7. Line 153-163: The authors take upregulation of har and haoAB as proof of hydroxylamine stress. Please report the
quantified fold changes explicitly, not only in the supplementary table, and if possible, include direct measurements of
hydroxylamine accumulation. Likewise, for nitrite reductase overexpression, provide nitrite accumulation data. Although it
was mentioned that nitrite builds up due to enhanced hydroxylamine oxidation and hampers metabolism, I could not find
supporting quantitative values. Without metabolite data, these conclusions remain incomplete.
8. For the amtA/amtB knockout, please provide ammonium uptake assays or intracellular NH4+ quantification to confirm that
growth was not limited by transport.
9. Arabinose concentrations vary between figures/sections (0.4 g/L in SI fig, 0.1 g/L in main text. Please resolve and state
whether arabinose affects growth beyond induction (co-substrate or stress).
10. Please provide gas flow rate (vvm), CH4:O2 ratio, pressure, antifoam policy, and kLa, together with full gas mass
balances (CH4/O2 in, CO2 out). The reported Yx/CH4 = 1.09 g/g is unusually high, if possible please include raw
calculations.
11. In fermentation, feeding was stopped at around 30h due to cell decline. Please provide ammonia and hydroxylamine
profiles, pH, DO, and residuals to justify the <10 mM control band, and discuss whether oxygen transfer or by-products
ceased the cell growth.
12. Endotoxin is reported as <0.02 EU/mL, but PEC catalysts and neutralization may introduce trace metals or chloride.
Please provide data for (Fe, Ni, Cu, Bi, V) and Cl⁻ levels for the NH4Cl stock and final broth, as these are critical for feed
applications.
13. Many supplementary figures can be combined together and can be labeled as A-B etc. for instance S. figure 9-11.
14. Line 213: The 1:1 protein:polysaccharide ratio should be supported with g/gDCW values.
15. Line 218: In Figure 3e–f, compare amino acid profiles statistically to fishmeal, egg, and milk; currently “comparable” is
qualitative.
16. Figures 5c and 5e show relative abundance changes; please include % values and p-values.
17. Supplementary Figure 25b: quantify fold changes of Klebsiella, Helicobacter, Alloprevotella.
18. Line 296-299: Clarify whether other metabolites (isovaleric acid, alanine, lithocholic acid acetate, myristic acid) were
significantly different after multiple-testing correction.
19. The Discussion section highlights 5-fold higher DCW and 18-fold productivity, but please contextualize with earlier
industrial methanotroph SCP benchmarks (e.g., Methylococcus capsulatus data).
20. The claim of “replacing antibiotics and vaccines with feed ingredients” does not seem appropriate. Please change the
phrase.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This study makes important contributions by developing a workable combined chemical-biological method to convert
scattered methane into functional animal nutrients on-site: it successfully addresses the key problem of methanotrophic
bacteria using ammonia inefficiently, and this solution directly boosts cell production. The study also verifies that the "gas-to-
protein" process works, and further shows the microbial nutrient helps improve DSS-induced colitis in mice, specifically by
strengthening the intestinal barrier, maintaining the balance of gut bacteria, and promoting the production of gut metabolites.
These findings lay a solid foundation for the application of methane-derived microbial cell proteins as value-added feed
additives. Given the novelty of the work and its important findings, I would recommend accepting the manuscript for
publication after addressing the following minor revisions.
1.Explain the reason for choosing the DSS-induced colitis mouse model to test how the cell mass from methanotrophic
bacteria helps improve gut health. Explain why this model is suitable for checking whether the tested material can work as a
probiotic.
2.The current way to analyze colon tissue (looking at its structure under a microscope) only uses visual checks to describe
features, which can lead to personal bias when judging key issues (e.g., stomach lining sores, intestinal gland damage,
inflammatory cell buildup). Use a set standard scoring method to measure how much the colon tissue is damaged. Also, mark the damaged areas in Figure 4d so they’re easier to see.
3.Provide more discussion about how the specific gut bacteria found relate to the gut’s metabolic products (e.g., TCDCA,
suberic acid). This will better support the proposed reasons behind how the material improves gut health.
4.Show how the special traits of the cell mass production process (the early steps) connect to the observed benefits for gut
health. This link is needed to make the study’s story complete and logical.
5.To help readers fully understand and repeat the statistical checks of gut bacteria and metabolic products (e.g., data in
Supplementary Figure 21−29), authors should include the necessary descriptive details in the Supplementary Information
File.
6.In Methods section, clearly state how much of the test substance was used in the animal experiments. Also, give detailed
information on how this amount was decided—this is important to make sure the study can be repeated and to help readers
understand how the amount used affects the results.
7.Minor concerns:
1) Clarify the distinction between “ammonia” and “ammonium”, as the manuscript currently confuses these two substances.
2) Replace the term “M. sanxanigenens cell mass” with “methanotrophic cell protein”, which is used to describe the
microbial nutrient synthesized by methanotrophic bacteria. This will be more appropriate in this context and helps readers better
understand the product’s characteristics and functions.
3) Correct formatting inconsistencies in the manuscript: On page 13, line 339: Adjust “(TCDCA)” to “TCDCA”; In the legend
of Figure 4e: Capitalize “occludin” to “Occludin”.

Probiotic effects of nutritional cell protein on gut health
Recent studies have emphasized the promising benefits of MCP in promoting fish gut health. Here,
we employed a dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis mouse model, which adequately
simulated key pathological features of intestinal inflammation (relevant to human intestinal
disorders), including intestinal barrier disruption, inflammatory response, and gut microbiota
dysbiosis. The MCP was orally administered to evaluate its efficacy in ameliorating DSS-induced
colitis (Supplementary Figure 16 and Supplementary Figure 17a). Compared to the model group
(“+DSS” group), colitis mice treated with MCP (“+DSS,MCSP” group) exhibited significantly
reduced body weight loss (Figure 4a), lower disease activity index (DAI) score (Figure 4b and
Supplementary Table 5), and less colon shortening P(Figure 4c and Supplementary Figure 17c),
thereby contributing to a higher survival rate (SNupplementary Figure 17b).

mitigated DSS-induced structural integrity disruption of colonic tissue, as evidenced by reducing

expression of anti-inflammatory interleukin-10 (IL-10) compared to mice with colitis (Figure 4g

alleviate colitis by restoring intestinal barrier and attenuating inflammations in mice.
